title: React Internals & Fiber Architecture: Render & Commit Phases
description: Master React under the hood: the Fiber data structure, work loop, concurrent rendering, lane-based priority scheduling, and understanding how React updates the DOM without blocking the main thread.

data.text: The Fiber Reconciler & Concurrent Work Loop

In early versions of React (pre-v16), the reconciler operated synchronously via recursion (the 'Stack Reconciler'). If a component tree was deep or a state update was computationally intensive—such as re-rendering thousands of chat history nodes while streaming AI tokens—the browser main thread was locked, dropping frames and causing unresponsive input fields. React 16 completely rewrote the core engine into Fiber: a virtual call stack where work units can be paused, prioritized, aborted, and resumed across browser animation frames.

data.text: Every React element corresponds to an internal Fiber node. Rather than a recursive tree, fibers form a singly-linked list with three primary pointers: `child` (points to the first child), `sibling` (points to the next sibling), and `return` (points to the parent fiber). This structure allows React to traverse and pause work anywhere without maintaining a deep recursive call stack.

data.title: Conceptual TypeScript Fiber Representation
data.content: Understanding the internal fields of a Fiber node clarifies how React manages hooks and double buffering.

data.text: React borrows the double-buffering technique from graphics rendering. At any time, there are two fiber trees: `current` (the tree currently rendered on the screen) and `workInProgress` (the tree being assembled in memory during the render phase). If a render is aborted or superseded by higher-priority work, React simply discards the `workInProgress` tree without the user ever seeing half-rendered or inconsistent UI.

React 18 and 19 expose Fiber's lane-based priority scheduling directly to developers. By wrapping heavy non-urgent state updates in `useTransition`, you tell React that user typing, button clicks, and micro-animations should interrupt the heavy render.

data.title: React Fiber & Concurrency Best Practices
items: Keep render phase pure: never perform network requests or mutate globals inside component bodies
Use useTransition for non-urgent UI updates (filtering lists, searching history, tab switching)
Use useDeferredValue for lagging expensive child components behind immediate prop changes
Ensure keys are stable, unique IDs across sibling items so reconciliation can preserve DOM nodes
Never call hooks conditionally; hooks rely on strict linked-list ordering inside Fiber.memoizedState
Leverage React 19 Actions for asynchronous state transitions and automatic pending state handling

data.title: Summary & Next Steps
points: Fiber replaced the synchronous call stack with an interruptible linked-list work loop.
Double buffering ensures incomplete UI renders are never committed to the screen.
useTransition and useDeferredValue unlock concurrent lane scheduling for smooth 60fps UIs.
Next, we master Custom Hook design patterns for reusable, composable React logic.
data.takeaway: Understanding React Fiber transforms performance optimization from guesswork into engineering: keep renders pure, prioritize urgent input, and defer heavy UI workloads.
